overview: Seven Valais districts developed a republic from older institutions shared with the bishop of Sion. Their decisive assertion of sovereignty began in 1613. This atlas’s 1530 to 1800 span includes that earlier arrangement and extends beyond the republic’s end in 1798.

periods.title: Districts and bishop
periods.summary: The seven districts shared political space with the prince-bishop of Sion.

periods.title: Republican institutions
periods.summary: District elites progressively displaced the bishop’s secular authority.

periods.title: Commerce and political conflict
periods.summary: Stockalper’s ascendancy and downfall exposed tensions within the governing elite.

items.text: Communes elected local officials and sent instructed representatives to district councils. Delegates could not simply invent new policies: unexpected questions needed consultation at home. Political participation nevertheless became increasingly concentrated among influential families.

The seven districts governed Monthey and Saint-Maurice as subject territories. Governors served rotating two-year terms and accounted to the common diet. The republic therefore combined self-government for its ruling districts with unequal status for other valley communities.

Mountain farming depended on channels called bisses, or Suonen in the German-speaking upper valley. Irrigation helped meadows grow hay for livestock through winter. Members of water associations contributed labor according to their landholdings: getting water to a field was also a collective obligation.

The Grand Bisse de Vex was already an inherited piece of infrastructure: a surviving act dates its creation to 1453. A 1476 agreement regulated water sharing and maintenance duties across communities. Its twelve-kilometer course carried water through several jurisdictions; the water needed agreements as well as a downhill route.

Rye bread had a long place in Valais food, with written evidence reaching back to 1209. Rye tolerated difficult mountain conditions, and the bread’s keeping qualities made it valuable in valley households. Today’s protected commercial designation is much newer than this food tradition.

A recipe preserved in the Stockalper cookbook mixes chopped liver with eggs, cream, ginger, pepper, nutmeg and raisins before baking. The combination may surprise a modern sandwich-maker. It records an elaborate kitchen preparation, rather than a menu that every farming family could afford.

Brig’s Jesuit college occupied a new building in 1673 and included boarding accommodation. Its 1686 agreement provided for a full secondary course, logic and moral theology. Enrollment fluctuated between roughly eighty and 150 pupils before 1738: this was a particular boys’ institution, not universal schooling.

Gaspard Stockalper gained the Valais salt monopoly in 1647, improved the Simplon route and built a canal between Vouvry and Collombey in 1651 to 1659. Transport, mining, lending and military business were connected parts of his fortune. Control over routes and essential supplies could translate into political power.

Stockalper’s palace at Brig, begun after 1649, placed an arcaded courtyard beside three massive stone towers with onion-shaped roofs. Its size advertised the wealth of a merchant and officeholder in a small Alpine town. The surviving building makes his ambition unusually easy to see.

Writing sample: the cookbook dated 1581 in the Stockalper archive includes the early German instruction “Nembt ein leber”: “Take a liver.” This is wording from a preserved recipe, quoted in a modern scholarly-based transcription. Its spelling offers a tiny glimpse of written German used in a practical household text.

Stockalper became the republic’s leading magistrate in 1670, but powerful opponents in four districts moved against him in 1677 to 1678. He lost his public offices and part of his property. His story illustrates how quickly commercial dominance could become a political liability.

In 1798 the old subject relationship broke down. Lower Valais gained freedom, and a short-lived ten-district republic replaced the seven-district order before incorporation into the Helvetic Republic under French pressure.

ending.text: The seven-district republic ended in the upheaval of 1798, when Valais entered the Helvetic Republic. Later governments included another republic and a French department before Valais became a Swiss canton in 1815. These were new political arrangements; the atlas’s 1800 endpoint is a map convention.
